course_title: Ancient World Study Tour and Field School

learning_outcomes.description: Recognise, describe, and contextualise key features of the history, architecture, material culture, and landscape of ancient Rome and Italy.
Relate archaeological, material, and topographic evidence to major historical events, personalities, and institutions in the Roman world.
Understand the ways in which the later use, restoration, and reception of ancient remains shapes our understanding of ancient art, architecture, and culture.

assessments.task_description:
Task description: Students are required to submit two diary entries on sites and/or objects experienced during each week of the study tour (six entries in total). Diary entries should provide a genuine reflection on your experience, identify and explain the significance of the site or object, and engage critically with its interpretation and reception. Where relevant, students should draw connections between their observations and the representations of places, monuments, and objects encountered in preparatory readings, including Pausanias’ Descriptions of Greece. Entries should be clear, concise, and appropriate to the diary genre, with references included where necessary.

Format: Students may choose the format of their diary entries. Possible formats include a written diary, podcast, video blog, or social media platform (e.g. Instagram or YouTube). Any social media account used for this assessment must be set to private.

Students may not use the site selected for their presentation as the subject of a diary entry. Creativity in format and presentation is encouraged but will not form part of the assessment criteria.

Submission: Students must submit both the diary entries themselves (e.g. PDFs, MP4 files, or links to private social media content) and a completed transcript template, available on Blackboard.

Each diary entry should be approximately 300 words (±10%), resulting in a total transcript length of approximately 1,800 words (±10%), excluding references and bibliography.

For audio-visual or social media formats, the transcript should contain the spoken or written content of each entry.

References and a bibliography must be included in the transcript template. The transcript must use the referencing style specified in the Classics and Ancient History Study Guide available on Blackboard.

This task has been designed to be challenging, authentic and complex. Whilst students may use AI and/or MT technologies, successful completion of assessment in this course will require students to critically engage in specific contexts and tasks for which artificial intelligence will provide only limited support and guidance. A failure to reference generative AI or MT use may constitute student misconduct under the Student Code of Conduct. To pass this assessment, students will be required to demonstrate detailed comprehension of their written submission independent of AI and MT tools.

assessments.task_description:
Task description: Students will prepare a handout, give an on-site oral presentation, and answer questions about two assigned topics on a monument, event, person, and/or location important to the history of ancient Greece.

Presentation + Handout (50%):

Presentations: Students will give two on-site oral presentations in Greece to the group on a monument, event, person, and/or location important to some aspect of ancient or late antiquity Greek art, architecture, and/or history, as listed in the Course Profile. Presentations should last about 10 minutes, with students prepared to answer questions afterwards.

Students are required to sign up for two (2) presentation topics at the start of the semester. The two topics must be selected from different weeks of the tour. Sudents may not choose both presentation topics from the same week.

Presentation topic preferences will be submitted via Microsoft Forms. Students must nominate three preferred presentation topics for each week of the tour by the start of Summer Semester, 30 November 2026. Students will be allocated two presentation topics, scheduled in different weeks of the program, based on their preferences and overall course requirements. While every effort will be made to accommodate student preferences, specific topic allocations cannot be guaranteed. Students who do not submit their preferences by the end of Week 1 will be allocated topics at the discretion of the course coordinator. Once allocations have been finalised, changes will only be permitted where a suitable alternative topic remains available.

Handout: Students will prepare a handout on their allocated topics and upload it to Blackboard before the study tour. Each handout should be 1 to 2 pages (can be double sided) and should incorporate relevant texts, images and a short bibliography.

Students must refer to the handout and the site at least once during their presentation.

Your presentation must cover:

  1. Author and creation – who, when, where, if known.
  2. Historical context – historical background of the site/object, discuss specific characters or events related to the site/object.
  3. Source analysis – discuss use and function of the site/object, analyse the features and spatial context, identify key ancient evidence, either literary, material or physical, relevant for understanding the site/object.
  4. Historical significance and legacy – did the site have longevity/a legacy, why was it important to the Greek people, what does this site tell us about ancient Greeks, has the site/object changed from Antiquity to present day through human interference, weather, or preservation?


Q+A (50%): Students will be required to answer questions from the group, including the lecturer and tutor, after their presentation. The Q&A session will be 5-10 minutes in duration.

assessments.task_description:
While on tour, you are expected to participate in all scheduled activities, engage appropriately with fellow students and staff, and behave at all times in accordance with the UQ Code of Conduct.

As part of your participation in the course, you are expected to:

  • Arrive on time for all tour activities and transport connections.
  • Prepare for site and museum visits by reading the prescribed text from Pausanias and the relevant handout.
  • Engage with presentations delivered by fellow students and course staff.
  • Conduct yourself in a courteous, respectful, and professional manner.

Your Participation and Citizenship mark will also take into account your engagement in class discussions, including your attentiveness during presentations and the extent to which you contribute thoughtful, informed, and constructive questions and comments in discussion with fellow students and staff.

This assessment task is to be completed in-person.
